Why learn this stuff??

“Data types and Data Structures” – this sounds boring and intimidating. So why do we need this?

Well, these are fundamental concepts in programming, and they transcend R – they apply to any programming language.

  • Data types define the kind of data that a variable can hold and the operations that can be performed on that data. They inform the default behaviors and rules R uses for dealing with them. These are sometimes called “classes”.

  • Data structures are ways to organize and store data in a structured and efficient manner within a computer program. They allow you to group and manage related pieces of data together. Think of data structures as containers that hold data in specific formats to make it easier to work with that data.

Part 1: Data Types

The most often used classes are: numeric, integer, logical, character. We’ve seen a few of these last lab, but let’s go further:

  • numeric: also called double. By far the most common type in R; contains any number with or without a decimal.
  • integer: numeric data without decimals. This is used when you are certain that you will never create a variable that should contain decimals. Just add the letter L after the number to create an integer.
  • character: used to hold strings of text
  • complex: number is written with an “i” as the imaginary part. Less used.
  • raw: used to hold raw bytes1. Rarely used by most people.

Note: the raw and complex types are much less oftne used and we don’t go into them here, but you’ve been informed that they exist!

Numeric and Integer

Numeric

This is the default computational data type in R.

If you enter a number without a decimal point, R will automatically convert it into a numeric data type. Numeric values in R can hold any real number, including both integers and fractions, and even negative numbers. For example, 5, 23.5, and -3 are all numeric values.

mypi <- 3.14
print(mypi)
[1] 3.14

Note: because the number \(\pi\) is important, R has it built-in for you. Try typing pi and then ?pi in the space below. Also, check if pi == mypi.

mypi <- 3.14
print(mypi)
[1] 3.14
pi
[1] 3.141593
pi == mypi  #remeber, == means 'is the same as'
[1] FALSE

The reason they are not equal is that you rounded R to two decimals, whereas the built-in pi has more decimal points.

Checking data types

There are a few functions in R we can use to test the data type of the mypi variable we just made. is.numeric() and is.integer() return a simple TRUE or FALSE in answer to the prompt. class() and typeof(), on the other hand, are more general and will provide which data type the variable or object is.

Try these out here:

Integer

This data type in R is used to hold whole numbers. Unlike numeric values, integers cannot have a decimal point. You can create an integer in R by adding an ‘L’ suffix to a number, like this: 5L. Without the ‘L’, R would treat the object as numeric, not integer.

class_number <- 215L
typeof(class_number)
[1] "integer"
class_number2 <- 215
typeof(class_number2)
[1] "double"

Try to predict what will happen below. Then, run the code.You can also ask R if a given object is of a given type.

is.numeric(class_number)
[1] TRUE
is.numeric(class_number)
[1] TRUE

Logical

Logical data type in R is used to hold Boolean values: TRUE or FALSE. You can use logical operators like <, >, ==, etc, to generate logical values.

For example, the operation 5 > 3 will return TRUE because 5 is indeed greater than 3.

Try to predict what will happen below. Then, run the code.

pi > 3
[1] TRUE

If applied to a vector, functions like is.numeric() will ask the question to the entire vector, because a vector can only contain one type of element.

Try to predict what will happen below. Then, run the code.

myvec <- c(0, 1, 10, 20, 100)
is.numeric(myvec)
[1] TRUE
#
myvec2 <- as.integer(c(0, 1, 10, 20, 100))
is.numeric(myvec2)
[1] TRUE

Why is myvec2 also returning TRUE for the is.numeric() function?

  • is.numeric() is a general test for the “numberliness” of a vector and returns TRUE for both integer and double vectors. It is not a specific test for double vectors, which are often called numeric.2 It’s best to use typeof() if you must know whether a vector is numeric (double) or integer.

Note: FALSE/TRUE can be written as F/T, like so:

cashewIsCute <- TRUE

# is the same as

cashewIsCute2 <- T

# check
typeof(cashewIsCute)
[1] "logical"
typeof(cashewIsCute2)
[1] "logical"
cashewIsCute == cashewIsCute2
[1] TRUE

Attention: a common mistake when assigning TRUE or FALSE to an object is to use quotes. If you do that, R will interpret it as a string (character).

Try it: create a variable cashewIsCute3 with the value “TRUE” (in quotes). Then use typeof() to check it.

[1] "character"

Character

Character data type in R is used to hold strings of text. You can create a character string by enclosing text in quotes. For example, “Hello, World!” is a character string.

mystring <- "Hello, world"

The above example is a vector of 1 element only (“Hello, world”) but vectors can carry many elements, like this:

types_of_data <- c("Numeric", "Integer", "Logical", "Complex", "Character", "Raw")

Use the sandbox below to test these out. Create a different character vector and then ask is.character.

Note: you can convert a character vector into numeric if the elements happen to be numbers. The other way around also applies:

myvec <- c("1", "5", "10", "11")
is.numeric(myvec)
[1] FALSE
#
myvec2 <- as.numeric(myvec)  #
myvec2
[1]  1  5 10 11
is.numeric(myvec2)
[1] TRUE

We will see more about this later when discussing coercion.

Factors

Factors are very useful. Technically they are a modified data structure rather than a data type but this distinction is not terribly important for beginners.

Factors are great for storing categorical variables. E.g. Champions of the American Major League Soccer (or, for the rest of the world, football) in the past 10 years.(Note, the MLS also includes Canadian and Mexican teams.)

You could start off with a vector of which teams won each year.

# first position is 2022, second is 2021 and so on
mls_champions <- c("Los Angeles FC", "New York City FC", "Columbus Crew", "Seattle Sounders",
    "Atlanta United FC", "Toronto FC", "Seattle Sounders", "Portland Timbers", "Lost Angeles Galaxy")
length(mls_champions)  #check that there are 10 elements
class(mls_champions)  #check that class so far is character

And now you could convert this into a factor, since it is clearly a categorical variable. We will use, yes, you guessed it, as.factor():

mls_champions_factor <- as.factor(mls_champions)
is.factor(mls_champions)
print(mls_champions_factor)
is.factor(mls_champions_factor)

Try these out here:

You will notice that printing mls_champions_factor will spit out the vector, followed by 8 Levels: Atlanta United FC Columbus Crew Los Angeles FC Lost Angeles Galaxy New York City FC ... Toronto FC.

What this means is that the function as.factor() converted our simple character vector into a data type that is better equipped at handling categorical variables. The “levels” are the different categories observed in the data.

Some of the advantages of this will become clearer later on (next week) when we start plotting things and summarizing them.

Part 2: Data Structures

R’s base data structures can be organised by their dimensionality (1d, 2d, or nd) and whether they’re homogeneous (all contents must be of the same type) or heterogeneous (the contents can be of different types). This gives rise to the five data types most often used in data analysis:

R’s base data structures can be organised by their dimensionality (1d, 2d, or nd) and whether they’re homogeneous (all contents must be of the same type) or heterogeneous (the contents can be of different types). This gives rise to the five data types most often used in data analysis3:

Dimensions All elements have same type More than one type of element
1d vector list
2d matrix data frame
nd array

Note: another type we use often, factor, is an important data structure created by setting attributes of an atomic vector.

Vectors - again!

You already learned about vectors in the last lesson. They are a sequence of data elements of the same basic type. They can be numeric, integer, character, or logical4. They are one-dimensional.

R loves vectors and tends to treat everything like a vector: even an object with only one element is a vector. E.g., a<-"A" is simply a vector of length 1, whereas b <- 1:10 is a vector of length 10. Try it:

a <- "A"
length(a)
[1] 1
b <- 1:10
length(b)
[1] 10

Note: in R, 1:10 is a nice shortcut that generates a sequence of integers from 1 to 10. The lengthier way of doing it is with the command seq(from, to, by), like this:

seq(from = 1, to = 10, by = 1)

Now try making a sequence from 0 to 1 with increments of 0.1 (hint, make sure you change by = accordingly:

Vectors can be named, meaning, each position receives some kind of name, so for instance, let’s say you have 5 chickens and you recorded the nr of eggs they laid today:

nr_eggs_laid <- c(1, 0, 5, 1, 2)
names(nr_eggs_laid)  #returns NULL because you have not named the vector elements
NULL
#
names(nr_eggs_laid) <- c("chick1", "chick2", "chick3", "chick4", "chick5")
names(nr_eggs_laid)
[1] "chick1" "chick2" "chick3" "chick4" "chick5"
nr_eggs_laid
chick1 chick2 chick3 chick4 chick5 
     1      0      5      1      2

ALL ELEMENTS OF A VECTOR MUST BE OF THE SAME TYPE!!*

So what happens if you try to bypass that?

Answer: coercion. I.e., if you try to place different types of data into a vector, R will convert all of them into the most flexible type among those you included, in this order from least to most flexible: logical, integer, double, character. Try to predict what coercions will happen below, then run the code:

# a character and a logical. What do you think will happen?
avector <- c("A", TRUE)
typeof(avector)
[1] "character"
avector
[1] "A"    "TRUE"

TRUE (logical) became “TRUE” (character).

Try to predict what coercions will happen below, then run the code:

# a character and a logical. What do you think will happen?
avector2 <- c("A", 2)
typeof(avector2)
[1] "character"
avector2
[1] "A" "2"

2 (numeric) became “2” (character)

Lists

Vectors come in two flavours: atomic vectors and lists. They have three common properties:

  • Type, typeof(), what it is.
  • Length, length(), how many elements it contains.
  • Attributes, attributes(), additional arbitrary metadata

All we’ve seen so far about vectors has been about atomic vectors. So what are lists?

Lists are different from atomic vectors because their elements can be of any type, including lists (yes, you heard that right, LISTS OF LISTS OF LISTS, etc). You construct lists by using list() instead of c():

So whereas this attempt at having different data types in one atomic vector results in coercion of 2 (double) into "2" (character):

# a character and a logical. What do you think will happen?
c("A", 2)

… the smae attempt but placing them into a list instead preserve their respective types:

# a character and a logical. What do you think will happen?
list("A", 2)

Notice that “A” is still “A” and 2 is still 2.

Here is a more elaborate example:

species_info_list <- list(SpeciesName = "Panthera leo", Population = 20000, Endangered = TRUE)
print(species_info_list)
$SpeciesName
[1] "Panthera leo"

$Population
[1] 20000

$Endangered
[1] TRUE

You can select any element on a list by using [[]], like so:

species_info_list[[1]]  #selects only species name
[1] "Panthera leo"

Or you can select an element on a list by its name. In this case you only need single brackets:

species_info_list["SpeciesName"]  #selects only species name
$SpeciesName
[1] "Panthera leo"

Lastly, you can use the $ to select any element on a list by its name:

species_info_list$SpeciesName  #selects only species name
[1] "Panthera leo"

Now you, use the three forms of indexing a list to get the endangered status element from the list above:

`

# first using [[]], no need to store in an object

# then using ['Name'], no need to store in an object


# then using $, no need to store in an object
[1] TRUE
$Endangered
[1] TRUE
[1] TRUE

Matrix

A matrix in R is a two-dimensional data structure, where each element is of the same atomic type. You can think of a matrix as a collection of vectors arranged side by side (for columns) or one on top of another (for rows). Here’s an example of a numeric matrix.

numeric_matrix <- matrix(1:6, nrow = 2, ncol = 3)
print(numeric_matrix)
     [,1] [,2] [,3]
[1,]    1    3    5
[2,]    2    4    6

Both dimensions of matrix can be named:

numeric_matrix <- matrix(1:6, nrow = 2, ncol = 3)
colnames(numeric_matrix) <- c("col1", "col2", "col3")
rownames(numeric_matrix) <- c("row1", "a random name")
numeric_matrix
              col1 col2 col3
row1             1    3    5
a random name    2    4    6

Data Frames

A data frame in R is a table or a two-dimensional array-like structure in which each column contains values of one variable and each row contains one set of values from each column. The data stored in a data frame can be of numeric, factor, or character type. You will use these a lot, this is just a brief introduction!

Importantly, all elements in one column are of the same type (say, character) but different columns can be of different types.

For instance, here is a data.frame:

# Create a data frame that holds information about various species
species_info <- data.frame(
  SpeciesName = c("Panthera leo", "Gorilla gorilla", "Homo sapiens"),
  CommonName = c("Lion", "Gorilla", "Human"),
  Family = c("Felidae", "Hominidae", "Hominidae"),
  GenomeSizeGB = c(2.8, 3.3, 3.2),  # in Giga Base Pairs
  Diet = c("Meat", "Herbivore", "Omnivore")
)
species_info
      SpeciesName CommonName    Family GenomeSizeGB      Diet
1    Panthera leo       Lion   Felidae          2.8      Meat
2 Gorilla gorilla    Gorilla Hominidae          3.3 Herbivore
3    Homo sapiens      Human Hominidae          3.2  Omnivore

Running str on this you can see the different types of columns you have:

str(species_info)
'data.frame':   3 obs. of  5 variables:
 $ SpeciesName : chr  "Panthera leo" "Gorilla gorilla" "Homo sapiens"
 $ CommonName  : chr  "Lion" "Gorilla" "Human"
 $ Family      : chr  "Felidae" "Hominidae" "Hominidae"
 $ GenomeSizeGB: num  2.8 3.3 3.2
 $ Diet        : chr  "Meat" "Herbivore" "Omnivore"

Let’s use the structure dataframe$columnname to select the column named “Family” and save that as a vector called family.

You can also use square brackets but $ allows you to see the name of the column you are extracting without counting which column you’re interested in in the original dataframe.
